name: Celtis

study_strategy.warning: Use the old Celtis ehrenbergiana name cautiously; current taxonomy does not map that legacy Texas usage cleanly to a fourth local species.

quick_split: C. laevigata — smoother leaves, unarmed tree
C. reticulata — rough leaves with strongly netted lower venation, unarmed
C. pallida — thorny dense shrub with small leaves

visual_gaps.note: Exact-species Commons files exist, but per-file license metadata was not reliably captured in this pass. Do not guess a license or promote scientific confidence. Leave the provisional learner photo-empty until a properly licensed exact image is locked.

look_here_first: Start with the entire plant: THORNY, densely branched shrub with small leaves suggests C. pallida; an UNARMED tree leads to the other three. Then photograph BOTH sides of a mature leaf. Smooth upper surface and relatively faint netting below suggest C. laevigata; very rough upper surface plus prominent NETWORK of raised veins below suggests C. reticulata; conspicuously WHITE-WOOLLY (tomentose) lower surface suggests provisional C. lindheimeri. Confirm hackberry genus by tracing three basal primary veins and looking for an individual fleshy drupe, not a dry elm samara.

shared_genus_pattern.features: Alternate simple leaves, often asymmetric bases with three prominent veins emerging near the petiole; small inconspicuous flowers and individual fleshy drupes enclosing a hard stone. Texture and vein relief of leaf surfaces often separate local members better than bark.
shared_genus_pattern.terms: SCABROUS = sandpaper-rough; RETICULATE = branching network of smaller veins; TOMENTOSE = densely felted with short hairs; DRUPE = fleshy fruit around hard stone; ASYMMETRIC BASE = sides of leaf blade meet stalk at different heights; THORN = sharp modified shoot, not an ordinary leaf tooth.
shared_genus_pattern.caution: Leaf-base asymmetry and basal veins establish a helpful Celtis pattern, not a species on their own. Bark wartiness is supportive rather than definitive.

comparison_matrix.laevigata: comparatively smooth; venation not strongly protruding
comparison_matrix.pallida: small leaf underside; confirm with thorny habit

comparison_matrix.reticulata: mostly entire or few teeth toward tip
comparison_matrix.pallida: usually small, entire to sparse teeth

comparison_matrix.lindheimeri: habitat supportive only, taxon under review
PROVISIONAL; one documented target county and differing treatments

field_key: 1. Sharp stem thorns + small leaves + dense shrub → C. pallida (granjeno/desert hackberry). Do not touch spines to test.
2. Unarmed tree: inspect whole mature leaf BOTH SIDES. Comparatively smooth leaf top, thin blades, relatively inconspicuous lower vein network → C. laevigata (sugarberry).
3. Very rough, thick upper blade with strongly raised netlike lower veins → C. reticulata (netleaf hackberry).
4. Lower blade densely white-woolly rather than simply net-veined → check provisional C. lindheimeri. Preserve its contested status; compare vouchers and authoritative treatments.
5. Mixed/intermediate leaves or uncertain surface details → Celtis sp. pending mature-leaf macro and fruit. Do not assign from corky bark alone.

visual_comparison.title: Celtis: thorns first, then TURN THE LEAF OVER
visual_comparison.teaching_order: whole growth form → thorn versus unarmed → mature upper leaf texture → underside net veins or felt hairs → base veins → individual drupe
